https://www.sbs.com.au/news/article/russ.text: Zelenskyy said Russia launched 35 missiles at Ukraine, including 27 ballistic missiles, and 185 drones. Only one ballistic missile was intercepted, "simply because there are no interceptors for the Patriot system", he said. More than a dozen explosions reverberated through the city during several waves of attacks, according to Reuters news agency witnesses. "Every package of ballistic missile interceptors saves the lives of our people. And every night without them results in more casualties," Zelenskyy said on the Telegram messaging app. With the war in its fifth year, fighting is raging along roughly 1,200 kilometres of front line. But Russian advances have slowed by more than half this year, and Ukraine has been launching strikes inside Russia, hitting its oil facilities, logistics sites, and weapons production. At the same time, Russia intensified its attacks on Kyiv and other Ukrainian cities, while Ukraine is chronically short of air defences capable of downing ballistic missiles, which travel at several times the speed of sound. Moscow and Kyiv both deny targeting civilians in the war launched by Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. Saturday's is the second major attack on Kyiv this week after strikes on Thursday killed nine people, including six members of one family in a village near Kryvyi Rih , and a suspected Russian cruise missile landed in Poland. Damage was recorded in seven districts across Kyiv, a city of about 3 million people, the Prosecutor's General Office said after Saturday's attacks. Zelenskyy said that fires broke out across Kyiv and 18 residential buildings, a school, the Lithuanian Embassy, and infrastructure facilities were damaged. The Lithuanian foreign ministry said windows at its embassy had broken, solar collectors were damaged, and the yard was scattered with debris. Ukrainian prosecutors said seven people were killed in the Darnytskyi district on the left bank of the Dnipro river and two more people died in the Solomyanskyi district on the right bank of the city. Dozens of people were injured, including four children who suffered multiple shrapnel wounds and lacerations. The attack comes as Ukraine presses its allies for Patriot air defences. Zelenskyy had met with US President Donald Trump on Wednesday for talks, partly to lobby Washington for licenses to produce Patriots domestically. The Ukrainian leader said following the meeting that Trump had agreed to license the production of the missiles to Kyiv. But the US president appeared to express reservations on Friday, saying that Washington would have to be "very careful" about the decision. On Saturday, Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiga said Russia's attacks showed Ukraine needed the weapon urgently. "It is the battle for the skies that will define the trajectory of this war. The stronger the air shield over Ukraine, the closer peace becomes," he said. Russia's invasion of Ukraine has sparked Europe's deadliest conflict since World War II. Tens of thousands have been killed and millions forced to flee their homes due to the fighting, while Moscow now occupies around a fifth of its neighbour — including Crimea, which it annexed in 2014. download our app subscribe to our newsletter

The Eastern Flank Working in Romania New Names on the Cover The Cooking Show Expat in Romania RRI Special The Sounds of Romania Voices from the Archives Our Shows Listeners’ Corner Romanian without Tears Sunday Show In the Spotlight Through the Looking Glass Change Makers Happening in Romania Music Time Artscape Weekend Edition On demand LISTEN HERE Useful information Things to know How to listen Forum QSL QSL-cards Homepage » Panoramice » Green Planet » The Green Belt of Bucharest The Green Belt of Bucharest Bucharest, one of Europe's most congested capitals, is taking steps toward sustainable urban development through a Green Belt project banner Terra Verde Daniel Onea , 25.09.2026, 14:00 The initiative aims to create a ring of vegetation around the city to combat pollution and the effects of climate change. Conceived to act as a veritable “oxygen mask” for a city stifled by traffic, the project has an estimated budget of 50 million euros. According to official documents, the first major expropriation and afforestation efforts are expected to begin in 2027, with the vision for full implementation extending to 2050. Beyond merely planting trees, the project aims to create vital ecological corridors and protect wetlands. Ciprian Gălușcă, Executive Director of the Climate Adaptation Platform, highlights the complexity of this undertaking as well as its vital role for the future of the metropolitan area: Ciprian Galusca: “The Green Belt is a project that is as ambitious as it is necessary. We are talking about developing vegetation that plays a key role in mitigating the negative effects of climate change, alongside a comprehensive spatial planning scheme for the Bucharest metropolitan area. We also aim to incorporate features that encourage recreation. We can envision a not-too-distant future where we might spend a full weekend near Bucharest within this Green Belt. During the summer, we could escape the city’s urban heat island effect by relaxing just 30 to 50 kilometers away. To bring this infrastructure to life, however, we first need a plan.” Currently, when we speak of the Green Belt, everyone has a slightly different understanding of the concept. Ciprian Gălușcă, Executive Director of the Climate Adaptation Platform, says that fears regarding a potential economic standstill caused by this ecological ring are completely unfounded. Ciprian Galusca: “For instance, some mayors in the metropolitan area worry that such a project might hinder local development. This is entirely untrue, as examples from Western Europe demonstrate the opposite: creating this type of infrastructure has spurred economic growth and laid the groundwork for a sustainable economy. A brief example: the Green Belt could become a meeting point where local producers and Bucharest residents—who might visit specific areas of the belt—can do their shopping. We could cycle to the forest or to one of the lakes near the city, stopping along the way at a market featuring local products. In other words, the first item on the agenda is to create a vision for this belt. Here, we need input from all relevant stakeholders: local authorities, businesses, Bucharest residents, and the communities living near the infrastructure. We must collectively define our destination and aspirations for the Green Belt, as this is a long-term process that will not be completed in just a year or two. We can look to the example of Vienna, which has been developing the green infrastructure around its capital for over a century. The Green Belt is a living entity; we need a strong, clear, and coherent development vision for it before moving to the implementation phase.” The foundation for this project already exists on the ground, but it requires a unified approach to become a functional network, notes the climate adaptation expert. Ciprian Galusca: “In the first phase, we are starting with the approximately 26,000 hectares of forest in Ilfov County. Currently, these are not managed in the way we would like for a ‘Green Belt’—that is, prioritizing social function, resilience, and climate adaptation. We therefore need to rethink the current forestry management model. Then, there is the network of lakes and pastures which, unfortunately, has lost its connectivity with the forests. Due to extensive real estate development and road infrastructure in the metropolitan area, we will need to find solutions to interconnect these natural zones. The goal is to make them accessible—in a sustainable manner—to local residents and all citizens of the metropolitan area. First and foremost, we must create a pleasant experience for those visiting these places. We have enough natural areas to launch this concept and to develop a vision, an operational plan, and an entity to manage this infrastructure. Subsequently, we can discuss expansion and new afforestation campaigns.” Successful European models demonstrate that environmental protection measures must be accelerated to safeguard the future of major urban centers, emphasizes Ciprian Gălușcă, Executive Director of the Climate Adaptation Platform. Ciprian Galusca: “Protecting the city is a priority. If we want a livable Bucharest in 20 or 30 years—or perhaps even sooner—we must take action. We should have done so already, but now we need to move much faster. For instance, following the deadly heatwaves of the early 2000s, Paris implemented a series of highly ambitious measures. They expanded urban green spaces and established rapid response plans for heatwaves. Today, they are far better prepared than they were 20 years ago. We do not need to reinvent the wheel. Vegetation, forests, and natural areas within and near communities represent the best and most accessible solutions for adapting to climate change.” Thus, the success of the Green Belt depends on close collaboration among all stakeholders and the courage of the authorities to transform existing natural spaces into a coherent network. It is a collective effort, essential not only for air quality but also for the future health of all residents in the Bucharest area. https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text: European Council President Antonio Costa, Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen in Brussels on October 16, 2026. Photograph: Nicolas Tucat/AFP/Getty Images View image in fullscreen European Council President Antonio Costa, Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen in Brussels on October 16, 2026. Photograph: Nicolas Tucat/AFP/Getty Images This Is Europe World news ​Europe stands by Ukraine – but how long can that last? As US support ebbs away, looming European elections and growing financial strains across the continent could fracture the precious coalition that has kept Ukraine afloat Jennifer Rankin Brussels correspondent Wed 21 Oct 2026 10.33 EDT Last modified on Wed 21 Oct 2026 12.24 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google E urope woke up last Friday to another belligerent outburst from Donald Trump – this time berating Ukraine’s wartime leader Volodymyr Zelenskyy again. Just a few days after his diesel deal with the Kremlin, the US president said Zelenskyy was more difficult to deal with than Vladimir Putin and blamed Ukraine’s leader for rocketing oil prices – without any reference to the impact of his own war on Iran. The contrast in Europe was obvious. When Zelenskyy walked into the multi-coloured summit room of the European Council headquarters in Brussels that Friday morning, the EU’s 27 leaders burst into applause, getting to their feet to offer big hugs and brisk handshakes. European Council president António Costa told Zelenskyy and the media: “This is no time to withdraw the support to Ukraine ,” calling instead for increased pressure on Russia. Zelenskyy was thankful, pointedly saying he was happy to have “huge support” from “real leaders”. The symbolism was powerful. As US support crumbles, Europe seems to be stepping up. According to the Kiel Institut’s Ukraine Support Tracker , Europe – including non-EU countries such as the UK and Norway – has spent €236bn supporting Ukraine from 2022 to April 2026, compared with a US outlay of €115bn. While Trump is weakening sanctions, Europe is promising more. The EU has passed 21 rounds of sanctions against Russia and last year agreed to raise a €90bn loan for Ukraine – an unprecedented sum for a non-member state. Meanwhile the EU has opened accession negotiations with Kyiv and given shelter to 4.4million Ukrainian refugees. Behind the declarations of Europe’s enduring support, the outlook is more complex and less encouraging for Ukraine, as it approaches its fifth winter since the launch of Russia’s all-out invasion. First, Europe is not able to replace US military dominance in areas such as intelligence. This was brutally exposed by the disruption to the US SpaceX technologies that Ukraine uses in frontline drone operations and air-defences protecting civilians from Russian air attacks. Zelenskyy said the US had intentionally throttled its Starlink satellite internet access, a charge that senior figures in the Trump administration have denied. Ukraine also depends on US-made Patriot interceptors capable of shooting down Russian ballistic missiles. Deepening the spat, Zelenskyy this week accused the Trump administration of preventing European countries from passing on their Patriot stocks to Ukraine. Secondly, Europe’s monetary support for Ukraine is not evenly spread. Germany is the second-largest donor, having spent €54bn since the start of the war, a particularly crucial contribution since Trump ceased virtually all new US funding. But a report from the Kiel Institut describes this funding as “sizeable but not exceptional” given the scale of the German economy. Four Nordic countries together have given more than Germany, even though they total only a third of Germany’s population, the researchers note. The EU’s other big economies, France and Italy, give less than Germany. The Nordic, Baltic and other north European states are Ukraine’s most generous donors when contributions are measured against national income, according to the Kiel Institut. Denmark, for instance, spends an equivalent to 4.17% of its gross domestic product supporting Ukraine, and Estonia 3.77%, compared with 1.49% spent by Germany, 1.1% by France, 1% by Italy and 0.86% by the UK. With Ukraine’s huge bill to defend itself growing, and Russia’s relentless attacks continuing to wreak a heavy toll, these more generous donors might arguably feel Europe’s biggest economies – and other western allies – could do more to shoulder these ever-rising costs. Top donors to Ukraine by percentage of GDP View image in fullscreen Financial aid from 24 January 2022 to 31 August 2026 as a % of a country’s 2021 GDP. Illustration: Guardian graphic/Source: Kiel Institute for the World Economy Thirdly, and most critically, Europe’s support for Ukraine could be reaching its limits, as Europe enters a supercycle of elections in which the far-right are expected to make gains. National votes are due in Spain, France, Poland and Italy, four of the five biggest EU member states by population. Mujtaba Rahman , managing director for Europe at the Eurasia Group, argued that the biggest risk for Ukraine is not Trump’s opinions, but the potential for European support to fragment. There is a risk 2027 will be the year “when political reality, electoral reality, policy reality, economic reality catches up with Europe and prevents it being able to go further in its support for Ukraine”, he said. France’s elections could be the most consequential. The far-right leader and frontrunner Marine Le Pen is seeking to present herself as the candidate to restore order and security, after days of rioting and looting across French cities. She has also vowed to cease aid to Ukraine within six months of taking office “because we simply cannot do it any more”. Speaking to the Financial Times (£) , Le Pen vowed to slash France’s contributions to the EU budget, which raises questions about a proposed €100bn fund for Ukraine in the upcoming 2028-34 budget cycle. Beyond Ukraine, her election could plunge the EU into a deep internal crisis that will consume political energies and attention. Putin’s ‘strategic patience’ rewarded? skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to This is Europe The most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environment after newsletter promotion View image in fullscreen US patience is running out with Ukraine as US special envoy Steve Witkoff meets with Vladimir Putin in Russia. Photograph: Kristina Solovyova/Reuters “European support for Ukraine is already fragmenting,” argued Rahman, who points out the €90bn loan for Ukraine was agreed by only 24 EU countries (Hungary, Czechia and Slovakia opted out). But a Le Pen victory could tilt the balance, especially if anti-Ukraine parties make gains in Spain, Poland and Italy. “Le Pen is the biggest gamechanger because she will provide cover for many other countries to say: ‘enough is enough, we can’t keep funding,’” Rahman said. That scenario paints “a really dark picture for Ukraine, a really sad picture for Ukraine” he said. “Because it’s not about Ukraine’s performance on the battlefield – Ukraine has done a remarkable job of holding the line. This is the risk Europe has been talking about for a very long time, and has promised Ukraine many times it would not allow to happen: that through strategic patience, Russia gains in the negotiating room what it has not been able to gain on the battlefield. And that is precisely the risk Ukraine is now confronting.” To head off this risk, EU leaders will seek to shore up support for Ukraine by agreeing another funding plan. The head of the European Commission, Ursula von der Leyen, confirmed that Kyiv has a €70bn funding gap in 2027, although she expects Ukraine’s other international partners to help raise the sum. Jana Kobzová, co-director of the European Security Programme at the European Council on Foreign Relations, said an EU leaders summit in December will be the moment when “we should have a clear idea and mechanism” on providing the €70bn for Ukraine ahead of key elections. “I think the urgency and the consciousness on the side of the European leaders is already there.” To some extent, EU Russia policy is protected, after a recent decision to keep sanctions in place for three years, avoiding the need for divisive rollover decisions every six months. But a Le Pen victory in six months’ time could lead to a bigger problem than financing Ukraine, suggests Kobzová. “If there is a huge shift in Europe as a result of these elections that are going to affect the way the EU itself works, then Ukraine might become collateral damage.” Guardian live Q&A View image in fullscreen Alexander Hurst and Rokhaya Diallo. The appearance comes just days after Meghan's estranged father, Thomas Markle, was charged over the alleged possession of child sexual abuse images. It marks the Duchess of Sussex's first public appearance since his arrest , bringing additional attention to an event focused on protecting children from online harm. The Brussels event focused on the risks children face on digital platforms and the experiences of families affected by online abuse. By meeting those families and addressing the issue at the European Parliament, Harry and Meghan drew attention to the importance of child safety in an increasingly digital world. General Dagvin Anderson: Advancing Nigeria-US Counterterrorism Cooperation through AFRICOM Life & Style | 2 weeks ago General Dagvin R.M. Anderson, the seventh commander of U.S. Africa Command (AFRICOM), has described the security partnership between Nigeria and the United States as strong and productive, citing the impact of joint counterterrorism efforts, including a reported increase of more than 200 per cent in ISIS defections following a May 2026 operation. In an exclusive interview with THISDAY on the sidelines of the just concluded Africa International Defence Exhibition (AFRIDEX) 2026 in Lagos, General Anderson discussed the gains from intelligence sharing and operational cooperation between the two countries, the need to strengthen regional security collaboration and the importance of addressing governance and development challenges alongside military operations in the fight against terrorism. Chiemelie Ezeobi brings excerpts: How would you assess the current security partnership between the United States and Nigeria, particularly in the fight against terrorism, insurgency and banditry? I think we’ve got an exceptionally good relationship right now, and we’ve been able to work together very well. I know the most public operation was what happened in May, but the partnership with the Nigerian Armed Forces and Nigerian intelligence was exceptional, and that’s what really enabled that partnership to happen and to take out the number two terrorist in the world for ISIS, and probably one of the most active terrorists in the world. And that, to me, the importance of that is the impact that’s had on the global ISIS network, and then the continued partnership that we’ve been able to build with Nigeria afterwards, and the incredible operations that Nigeria has continued to prosecute against ISIS post-operation. So I think right now, the relationship is very strong, and I look forward to continuing to develop it. What specific support is the United States providing Nigeria to combat Boko Haram, ISWAP and other terrorist groups operating in the North-East and North-West? So really, we look at what are those unique capabilities that the United States can bring. So some of it is intelligence, but also understanding of the terrorist network globally. And so Nigeria brings the regional and local understanding, while we bring the global network understanding, and together that becomes very powerful. And then there’s some specialized capabilities that the U.S. can help provide, and then just the experience. We’ve been fighting terrorism for over 20 years. We’ve learned a lot about how to integrate intelligence and operations, and how to make those operations more effective. And so that’s really what we’ve brought to Nigeria, because Nigeria has a very capable and professional military. And so it’s been very easy for us to partner with them and engage in a very constructive way, and then look at some areas where, from our experience over several decades of fighting terrorism, we can help with the training and expertise for Nigeria. But the ultimate goal is to help Nigeria to take care of the issue and be able to defend their own borders. And I think what we bring is just a very small piece, but it’s an important piece. Nigeria has received international security assistance for years, particularly under the Trump administration. However, terrorism, banditry and mass kidnappings remain persistent threats. What, specifically, must change in the US–Nigeria security partnership to deliver more tangible results for Nigerians? So, some of it is what we provide in the military is the security foundation and some of the basic security. But ultimately, for terrorism and insecurity, it needs to be an investment in governance, an investment in development. And to me, one of the things we’re exploring is how do we talk to commerce and industry more to look at what are those commercial opportunities that can create a market-driven development that can create sustainable growth and sustainable opportunity? And just the demographics of the entirety of the continent and Nigeria, the number of youth is growing rapidly. And so how do we look at ways to create opportunity so they don’t have to turn to terrorism or illegal activity? And so that’s not really what we in the military do directly. We can help with that security foundation to set conditions for that stability, because the stability is what allows investment and eventual prosperity. Given the evolving security threats in the Sahel and the withdrawal of Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger from ECOWAS, how is AFRICOM working with Nigeria to prevent terrorist groups from exploiting the regional security gaps created by these withdrawals? So, we are continuing to try to open dialogue with the AES states in the Sahel. So previously, we had very good relationships with Mali, Niger, and Burkina Faso. We are looking to reopen that dialogue because we have a common threat. I’m very heartened by what’s happened recently in Senegal, where ECOWAS and the AES states have met. I think that dialogue is going to be critical to bring them back into the fold of the West African community. And then for AFRICOM, again, what is it we can bring that’s unique from the U.S. and be able to engage with these partners to help provide some of the intelligence and understanding, and then to help them with some of the training as we’ve done in the past? So, I do think there’s an opportunity, but we need to reestablish the dialogue and communications first. US military assistance to Nigeria covers intelligence-sharing, surveillance technology, military equipment and specialised training. Are there new areas of cooperation being considered to help Nigeria address growing insecurity in the North-West and North-Central regions, beyond the traditional focus on the North-East? Yes. So, the raid in May was in the North-East, in Borno State. That was in the Lake Chad Basin. And so we’ve been working with the Nigerian Armed Forces, really, where they see the best benefit. So where we’ve been working is primarily up in the North-East and in the North-West. And then part of it is how do we look at the transit of the terrorists and interdict that? And so working with the local authorities as well to stop the flow of terrorist activity and movement. Beyond operational support, what additional assistance can AFRICOM provide to disrupt terrorist financing, arms trafficking and the movement of foreign fighters across Nigeria’s borders? That’s a very difficult challenge. That is a big one, and that’s probably one of the most critical areas to look at: how do we cut off the financing or interdict that financing? And so, again, this is where the partnership is really important, because we understand some things from a global scale and how ISIS and al-Qaeda move their money, and we have some cyber capabilities to look at that. But then it’s really understanding locally how are they moving the money, how are they laundering the money, or where is that money moving? And so that information sharing and that dialogue is absolutely critical to start interdicting and disrupting their finances. In practical terms, we bring expertise and understanding from across the global enterprise. And then we have unique cyber tools that we can apply to the global networks. And then working with Nigeria to help them accentuate or improve the impact of those capabilities here locally. So I think it’s a two-fold effort. Given Nigeria’s strategic position in the Gulf of Guinea, what additional support can AFRICOM provide to the Nigerian Navy and other security agencies to tackle maritime insecurity, protect critical offshore infrastructure and prevent criminal networks from exploiting the region’s waters? So in maritime domain awareness, understanding what’s happening out in not just the territorial waters, but out in the economic zone, is I think critical. We see many illicit activities happen out there, from piracy to smuggling, to drug trafficking. We also see illegal fishing and other things that are taking livelihoods away from the local populations. So just having an understanding of what’s happening out there, we think is critically important. We have, from the United States government, invested or helped invest across West Africa in that maritime domain awareness, from maritime operation centres to radars, to also harnessing some of the new technologies and tools that can help create an awareness of what’s happening in that space. And then, once you understand what’s in that space, what needs to be developed in order to disrupt it or to interdict it? And then that’s where we can partner with individual nations to see what can be most effective. How will the United States and Nigeria measure the effectiveness of their security cooperation? Is there a mechanism for assessing progress, identifying gaps and adjusting their joint strategy when expected results are not achieved? Sometimes they’re easier to measure, sometimes they’re harder. But there’s a gamut, I think. You need to look across different indicators to see if you’re having success. So one: how many folks are joining these organisations? The second, that we’ve seen since the operation in May, is over a 200 per cent increase in the number of defectors from ISIS. So I think that’s a measure of success, that folks are looking at this and saying, “This organisation, I don’t want to be a part of it anymore.” And the fact that Nigeria has a programme to bring them back into society and reintegrate them is important. And so those are areas of success. Obviously, reduction in attacks and violence, reduction in criminality—all of that are indicators, but a lot of those take time, and they lag the actual events. So I think part of it is being patient and understanding what are the things we need to look at holistically, and then measure that success. Looking ahead, what measurable security outcomes should Nigerians expect from the US–Nigeria defence partnership over the next 12 months I think one of the things we have really, we have limited resources at AFRICOM, and so how do we maximise those capabilities? And it’s really concentrating on those areas that have the most impact, primarily for what the threats are to our United States homeland, which is terrorism, and then finding partners who are willing and capable. And I think that’s been one of the reasons the relationship with Nigeria has grown so well, is because Nigeria has been very willing and very capable to take on this fight. And it’s just a little bit of help from the United States in some key areas. And so, to me, what do we expect? We expect partner nations to take that on and be willing to address the threat. But then I think the other piece that we talked about earlier is not just the security military side of it, but then the investment at the local level in governance, in education, and then the economic opportunities that attract the youth away from the terrorists and the criminality into constructive business and constructive nation-building. You know, one of the things here in Lagos that’s been pretty impressive to me is the energy. And it’s everywhere. And it’s this very entrepreneurial spirit that is very American, at least I see it, right, as American. But we see it here, and one of the things I had learned is “Lagos dey bubble.” And I had not heard that before, but Lagos is always bubbling, it’s always churning. Like New York. There’s energy like New York. And so someone told me, they said, “Well, if you can make it here, you can make it anywhere.” And so I think part of it is Nigeria has got a huge amount of opportunity and potential. How do you harness it, and how do you channel that into positive efforts? And so this is one of the things that, you know, what do you expect from Africa, from African partners, is this energy. How do you take the growing youth population and channel that energy for a positive effort? And to me, that’s what we all need to work on, but it has to be done locally. So, those expectations, does it also involve training for our personnel? Basically, what Nigeria requests, we look at being able to provide. There is some training. We did provide some training earlier in ISR and in targeting. We will continue to work where we can to provide targeted training for Nigerian forces. About General Anderson General Dagvin R.M. Anderson is the seventh commander of U.S. Africa Command (AFRICOM), headquartered in Stuttgart, Germany, responsible for leading U.S. military operations and activities across Africa to protect and advance American national interests. Before assuming command, he served as Director for Joint Force Development on the Joint Staff at the Pentagon. His previous assignments include Vice Director of Operations on the Joint Staff; Commander of Special Operations Command-Africa; Deputy Director for Operations at U.S. Indo-Pacific Command; Special Assistant to the Commander and Director of the Commander’s Strategic Initiative Group for United Nations Command-Combined Forces Command-U.S. Forces Korea; Senior Aviation Advisor for Counter-Terrorism Operations at the Office of the Under Secretary of Defense for Policy, Special Operations/Low-Intensity Conflict; and Deputy Director of the Commander’s Action Group at U.S. Special Operations Command. A command pilot with more than 3,400 flight hours, including 738 combat hours, he has commanded at five echelons, including Joint Task Force Quartz, which oversaw the repositioning of U.S. forces from Somalia. His academic honours include fellowships at Harvard University and Masaryk University in the Czech Republic.
